Account.summary: Account is the Auth.js core type for information about the provider used during authentication. It also includes TokenSet fields for provider-returned token data.
Account.explanation: Account describes the provider-specific connection used for authentication. It includes provider identity, provider type, and token-related values inherited from TokenSet, with some fields varying by provider.
Account.returns: An Account object describing the authentication provider connection and its provider-specific token or identity data.

interview.question: What does the Account type represent?
interview.answer: Account represents information about the provider used for a sign-in. It also extends TokenSet, so it can carry tokens returned by an OAuth provider.
interview.followUp: How would you distinguish an OAuth account from an email account? Use the account's provider and type fields; the type identifies the provider category.

interview.question: Which fields identify an account's provider?
interview.answer: The provider field identifies the configured provider, such as Google. The type field uses ProviderType and identifies the provider category.
interview.followUp: What additional value can the provider field have for credentials authentication? It identifies the configured credentials provider, while the account identifier is provider-specific.

interview.question: Why does Account vary by provider?
interview.answer: Account can contain token information because it extends TokenSet. The exact account identifier and related values depend on the provider type.
interview.followUp: Why should persistence code account for provider differences? OAuth, email, and credentials providers supply different identity and token data.

keyPoints: Account models the provider connection involved in authentication.
Its shape includes token-set data returned by OAuth providers.
The provider field stores the configured provider identifier.
The type field records the provider category through ProviderType.
Account identity values are interpreted according to the provider category.

adapter.summary: An Auth.js adapter is the data-access layer that normalizes user, account, session, and related authentication persistence behind a common interface. Pass an adapter object, or configure one through an adapter factory, in Auth.js options.
adapter.explanation: An adapter connects Auth.js to a data source through methods that implement the common user, account, session, and passwordless-authentication operations. Supply either an adapter object directly or invoke an adapter factory with its configuration, then pass the result as the adapter option.

parameters.description: Adapter implementation or an adapter factory result, supplied through Auth.js configuration.

example.explanation: Pass the adapter object to Auth.js through the adapter option.

useCases.title: Integrate a custom data source
useCases.scenario: The chosen database or service has no official Auth.js integration.

useCases.title: Support passwordless flows
useCases.scenario: The application uses passwordless authentication and must persist its authentication records.

interview.question: What problem does an Auth.js adapter solve?
interview.answer: An adapter is an object whose methods read and write a data source using interfaces Auth.js understands. It lets Auth.js create, update, and delete users, link accounts, manage sessions, and support passwordless authentication.
interview.followUp: How can an application use a data solution without an official adapter? Implement an Auth.js-compatible adapter, commonly as a factory that receives a database or ORM client and returns the required methods.

interview.question: How is an adapter supplied to Auth.js?
interview.answer: Configure it with the adapter option in Auth.js. The value can be an adapter object directly, or the result of calling an adapter factory with configuration.
interview.followUp: Why might the factory form be useful? It allows the adapter to capture a client or other integration-specific configuration while exposing the standard adapter interface.

interview.question: Why can Auth.js support different kinds of data layers?
interview.answer: Adapters normalize different data layers behind common interfaces, so Auth.js can work with databases, ORMs, backend APIs, or HTTP clients. The adapter methods perform operations such as user management, account linking, session handling, and passwordless login support.
interview.followUp: What should be implemented first in a minimal adapter? Implement only the methods required by the authentication flows the application actually uses, while keeping their behavior compatible with the Adapter interface.

keyPoints: An adapter is a method-bearing object that reads and writes the application's authentication data source.
The common interface lets Auth.js work across different data-layer technologies.
Its methods cover the persistence work required by authentication flows.
User lifecycle operations are part of the adapter contract.
Adapters manage associations between provider accounts and users.
Session persistence and retrieval can be delegated to the adapter.
gotchas: Check the official adapter list before building a custom adapter; an existing integration may already meet your needs.
Creating a custom adapter is usually unnecessary when your database already has an official adapter.

AdapterAccount.summary: AdapterAccount describes an account record managed by an Auth.js adapter. It links a user to a provider and carries the provider-specific account identity used by adapter operations.
AdapterAccount.explanation: AdapterAccount is the adapter-facing account shape for connecting a user with an authentication provider. It includes the provider-specific identity, account kind, and owning user, while also allowing account token data inherited from the broader Account model.
AdapterAccount.returns: An adapter account record describing a user’s connection to a provider.

interview.question: What does AdapterAccount represent?
interview.answer: AdapterAccount is the account type used by Auth.js adapters. It models a provider connection belonging to a user and is returned by adapter operations such as getAccount.
interview.followUp: How should getAccount signal that no record exists? It should return null rather than fabricate an AdapterAccount.

interview.question: Can one user have multiple AdapterAccount values?
interview.answer: An account connects a user to a provider. Auth.js documents OAuth/OIDC and email accounts as account categories, and one user may have several accounts.
interview.followUp: Why is provider identity needed? It distinguishes the same user’s separate external or authentication-provider connections.

interview.question: How is AdapterAccount used by an adapter?
interview.answer: AdapterAccount is related to Account and carries provider information plus adapter ownership data, including the user associated with the account. Adapter methods use it when reading and writing account records.
interview.followUp: Which adapter operation commonly reads it? getAccount takes a provider account ID and provider and returns an AdapterAccount or null.

keyPoints: The type models the relationship between an Auth.js user and an authentication provider.
The documentation distinguishes account categories including OAuth/OIDC and email accounts.
OAuth/OIDC account records are created during sign-in through an OAuth provider.
Email-provider sign-ins create the corresponding email account record.
Adapter account retrieval identifies a record using both its provider account ID and provider.
The provider field identifies which authentication provider owns the connection.
gotchas: Adapter lookup methods may return null when no matching account exists; do not treat a missing account as an AdapterAccount.
Do not assume a user has only one AdapterAccount; account records represent separate provider connections.

AdapterSession.explanation: AdapterSession is the database-backed session shape used by Auth.js adapters. It ties a user to a session token and records the absolute expiry time; adapter methods can return it directly or together with the associated user.

interview.question: What does AdapterSession represent, and which fields does it contain?
interview.answer: AdapterSession represents a persisted user session for an Auth.js adapter. Its core fields are an expiration date, a session token, and the user ID.
interview.followUp: Why is the token needed? It provides the value used to find the stored session when the database strategy is active.

interview.question: How is AdapterSession used by createSession?
interview.answer: An adapter's createSession method accepts a session object containing expires, sessionToken, and userId, then returns an Awaitable<AdapterSession>. This lets the adapter persist the session and provide the resulting session object.
interview.followUp: What should getSessionAndUser return? It may return null, or an object containing both an AdapterSession and an AdapterUser.

interview.question: How does AdapterSession participate in database-session lookup?
interview.answer: With the database strategy, the session cookie contains the sessionToken, which Auth.js uses to look up the session in the database. The stored AdapterSession supplies the associated user and expiry information.
interview.followUp: How can a project avoid database session storage? Explicitly configure the JWT strategy instead of relying on the adapter-default database strategy.

keyPoints: It models the persisted state for a user's active sign-in.
The expires field is an absolute Date marking when the session becomes invalid.
sessionToken is the lookup identifier for the stored session and should be generated securely.
The session token is kept in a secure, HTTP-only client cookie when database sessions are used.
userId associates the persisted session with its database user record.
AdapterSession can be returned alongside AdapterUser by getSessionAndUser for a combined lookup.
gotchas: Reading a still-valid session can extend its lifetime according to the configured maxAge and updateAge settings.

AdapterUser.summary: AdapterUser is the database-facing user shape used by an Auth.js adapter. It represents someone who can sign in and carries the identity data needed to associate that person with accounts and authentication records.
AdapterUser.explanation: AdapterUser is the database-backed user shape used by Auth.js adapters. It identifies someone who can sign in and includes the required identifier, email, and email-verification state, with optional profile fields such as name and image.
AdapterUser.returns: An AdapterUser value representing a sign-in-capable user.

  email: "ada@example.com",
  emailVerified: null,
  name: "Ada Lovelace",
  image: null,
}

console.log(user.id)
example.explanation: Creates a value that satisfies the adapter user shape.

interview.question: What does AdapterUser represent?
interview.answer: AdapterUser is the user representation returned by an Auth.js adapter and represents a person who can sign in. Adapter operations such as creating or updating a database user return this shape.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from User? User is the provider/profile-facing shape, while AdapterUser is the adapter/database-facing shape and includes the adapter-required identity fields.

interview.question: Which information does an AdapterUser contain?
interview.answer: Its required identity data includes a unique user identifier, an email address, and the email verification value. Optional profile information can include a display name and image.
interview.followUp: Why is the identifier essential? Adapter operations use it to retrieve, update, delete, and associate related records with the user.

interview.question: When is an AdapterUser created?
interview.answer: When a user is absent, Auth.js can create the user on the first sign-in using identity-provider profile data. It also creates and links the corresponding provider account.
interview.followUp: What should an adapter support beyond users? It should also link and unlink accounts and handle active sessions and passwordless authentication.

keyPoints: AdapterUser models an application person who is allowed to authenticate.
Initial user data comes from the identity provider's returned profile information.
The provider account is associated with the created user.
The user has a unique identifier used to distinguish the database record.
gotchas: The adapter may create the user during the first sign-in when no matching user exists.
For an identity-provider sign-in, the provider account is linked to the newly created user.

Apple.explanation: Apple is a built-in OAuth provider for Auth.js. Add the provider to the providers array, configure the required environment variables, and use the provider’s callback endpoint for the Apple developer configuration.

example.explanation: Register the built-in Apple provider in a NextAuth configuration; supply AUTH_APPLE_ID and AUTH_APPLE_SECRET in the environment.

useCases.scenario: Users authenticate through Apple ID in a Next.js application.

interview.question: How is Apple added to an Auth.js configuration?
interview.answer: Import Apple from the framework-specific provider package and include Apple in the Auth.js providers array. The standard environment variables are AUTH_APPLE_ID and AUTH_APPLE_SECRET.
interview.followUp: What callback URL should be registered? Use the application’s HTTPS callback endpoint, such as https://example.com/api/auth/callback/apple for Next.js.

interview.question: What callback URL does Apple use?
interview.answer: Apple uses the callback path ending in /callback/apple. In a Next.js application, the documented form is https://example.com/api/auth/callback/apple.
interview.followUp: What deployment restriction applies? Apple does not support localhost or HTTP callback URLs, so the registered URL must be a live HTTPS URL.

interview.question: What makes Apple’s client secret and profile behavior special?
interview.answer: The client secret is not an ordinary static password: Apple requires it to be a JWT. The documented npx auth add apple command can help generate the required credentials and write the environment variables.
interview.followUp: Why should the initial profile be stored? Apple supplies the user’s name and email only on the first consent, so later sign-ins may omit them.

keyPoints: Auth.js includes Apple as a built-in sign-in integration.
The provider reads AUTH_APPLE_ID and AUTH_APPLE_SECRET as its documented environment variables.
Next.js applications use an Apple callback URL ending in /api/auth/callback/apple.
The built-in provider supplies default OAuth settings, which can be overridden when needed.
gotchas: Do not use Auth.js redirect-proxy deployments with Apple.
Apple sign-in requires a live HTTPS URL rather than localhost or plain HTTP.
The Apple client secret must be a JWT; Auth.js provides a CLI helper to generate one.
Persist the initial profile data because Apple may not provide the name and email again.

auth.summary: Auth.js’s Next.js auth function is a universal server-side authentication API. Export it from NextAuth configuration, call it to read the session, or use it to wrap handlers and inspect request authentication.
auth.explanation: In a Next.js application, NextAuth returns an auth function from the central configuration. Calling it without arguments reads the current session, while wrapping a route handler exposes the session as req.auth; the same universal method can be used across middleware, server components, route handlers, and API routes.
auth.returns: Session or null when called without arguments; wrapped request handlers receive req.auth containing the authenticated user or token, if any.

interview.question: What is the purpose of auth in Auth.js for Next.js?
interview.answer: auth is the universal Next.js method returned by NextAuth. It can be used in middleware, server components, route handlers, and Edge or Node.js API routes to access authentication state.
interview.followUp: How can an API route use it? Wrap the handler with auth, then read the authenticated value from req.auth.

interview.question: How is auth initialized and called?
interview.answer: Create an auth.ts configuration file, initialize NextAuth there, and export auth with the other returned helpers. Server-side code can then call await auth() to obtain the session.
interview.followUp: Why centralize this configuration? The exported function is reusable across the supported Next.js execution contexts instead of requiring separate session APIs.

interview.question: How does auth protect API routes?
interview.answer: For a route handler, auth can wrap the handler function. The request receives an auth property containing the authenticated user or token when available, or null otherwise.
interview.followUp: How is general authorization configured? Auth.js performs authentication through the callbacks.authorized callback.

keyPoints: auth provides one shared Next.js API for working with the current authentication state.
The function is designed for middleware, server components, app route handlers, and both Edge and Node API routes.
NextAuth returns auth alongside other helpers, so export it from the central configuration file.
Calling auth with no arguments asynchronously retrieves the current session for server-side code.
The authenticated request value may be a Session or null, depending on whether a user or token is present.
gotchas: Route protection decisions are handled through the authorized callback, so configure that callback when authentication should allow or deny access.
When auth wraps an API route handler, inspect req.auth rather than expecting the session as a separate argument.

interview.question: What are the input and output of Auth?
interview.answer: Auth is the main entry point of Auth.js Core. It receives a Web-standard Request and returns a Web-standard Response asynchronously.
interview.followUp: How can a caller verify the result type? The documentation’s example checks that the result is an instance of Response.

interview.question: How is Auth configured when called directly?
interview.answer: Import Auth from @auth/core and call it with the request followed by an Auth configuration object. The configuration can include settings such as providers, secret, and trustHost.
interview.followUp: What should be supplied for application-specific authentication behavior? Configure the Auth options object, including the providers and other required settings for the deployment.

interview.question: When would an application use Auth directly?
interview.answer: Auth is designed as core functionality for Auth.js and is primarily used to build framework-specific packages, although applications can call it directly.
interview.followUp: Why is direct use portable? Because the API is based on standard Request and Response Web APIs rather than a framework-specific transport type.

keyPoints: Auth serves as the central low-level entry point for Auth.js Core.
Its contract is a Web-standard Request in and a Response out.
Because the call is awaited, application code should treat handling as asynchronous.
The function is imported as a named export from the @auth/core package.
The configuration object can declare providers, a secret, and whether the host is trusted.
gotchas: Pass Web-standard Request objects and handle the returned Web-standard Response rather than framework-specific request or response types.
Auth is the low-level core entry point; framework integrations may provide a more convenient wrapper.

interview.question: How is Auth0 added to a Next.js Auth.js configuration?
interview.answer: Auth0 is supplied as a built-in provider by importing it from the framework-specific providers package and placing it in the `providers` array. In Next.js, the standard setup uses `Auth0` directly, while explicit `clientId` and `clientSecret` configuration is also supported.
interview.followUp: How would you customize the built-in provider? Call `Auth0` with configuration overrides; Auth.js merges those overrides with the provider defaults.

interview.question: Which environment variables does the Auth0 provider use?
interview.answer: The documented environment variables are `AUTH_AUTH0_ID` and `AUTH_AUTH0_SECRET`. Auth.js uses these credentials for the Auth0 integration when the provider is configured.
interview.followUp: What URL must be configured in Auth0? Set the application callback to `https://example.com/api/auth/callback/auth0`, adjusted for the deployed origin.

interview.question: What callback URL should an Auth0 Next.js application register?
interview.answer: The provider's callback endpoint ends in `/callback/auth0`, because `auth0` is the provider identifier used in the route. For Next.js, the documented path is `/api/auth/callback/auth0`.
interview.followUp: Why does the identifier matter beyond the callback URL? Provider identifiers uniquely identify entries in `AuthConfig.providers` and are also used in URLs.

keyPoints: Auth.js includes Auth0 as a built-in sign-in integration.
The provider documents `AUTH_AUTH0_ID` and `AUTH_AUTH0_SECRET` as its environment-variable credentials.
The Next.js callback endpoint uses the `/api/auth/callback/auth0` path.
The provider supplies defaults, so a basic setup can use `Auth0` without a configuration object.
When customization is needed, the provider accepts an OIDC user configuration parameter typed for `Auth0Profile`.
gotchas: The Auth0 application must use the callback URL that matches the deployed Auth.js route; for the Next.js setup, this is the API callback path.

interview.question: What is AuthConfig used for?
interview.answer: AuthConfig is the type used to configure the core Auth method. A configuration object can be passed to Auth, as shown in the core reference.
interview.followUp: Why might configuration be split across files? A shared object can omit an adapter for edge-compatible usage, while the server-side Auth instance adds the adapter separately.

interview.question: How do you apply an AuthConfig?
interview.answer: Define an object typed as AuthConfig and provide it to Auth. The core reference demonstrates importing the type from @auth/core and passing the object to Auth.

interview.question: Is AuthConfig itself an Auth.js instance?
interview.answer: AuthConfig describes configuration rather than creating an Auth instance by itself. The installation documentation recommends an auth.ts configuration file where library behavior and custom authentication logic are specified.

keyPoints: AuthConfig describes the options used to configure the core Auth method.
The core Auth function is the main entry point and accepts the configuration object.
Declare a configuration object with the AuthConfig type when you want explicit type checking.

interview.question: How do you configure Authentik in Auth.js?
interview.answer: Authentik is configured by calling the built-in provider with clientId, clientSecret, and issuer, then placing the result in Auth.js's providers array. Auth.js treats the integration as OpenID Connect by default.
interview.followUp: What must the issuer URL contain? It must include the Authentik application slug and must not end with a slash.

interview.question: What callback URL should an Authentik application use?
interview.answer: The callback endpoint uses the Authentik provider identifier: /api/auth/callback/authentik in the standard Next.js example. This URL must be registered with the Authentik application.
interview.followUp: Why does the callback use authentik? The provider's built-in identifier determines the callback path segment.

interview.question: What does the Authentik provider factory return?
interview.answer: The provider accepts OAuthUserConfig options and returns an OAuthConfig. Its defaults can be customized when the built-in configuration does not match the deployment.
interview.followUp: How can defaults be changed? Pass provider options in the Authentik call, using Auth.js's built-in provider customization approach.

keyPoints: Auth.js includes Authentik as a built-in provider, so no custom provider definition is needed.
The integration follows OpenID Connect assumptions unless its configuration is overridden.
The documented environment-variable names provide the Authentik client ID, secret, and issuer.

Provider options can override the built-in configuration for deployment-specific requirements.

interview.question: What is AuthError?
interview.answer: AuthError is Auth.js’s base error class and extends Error. It provides a type property containing the applicable ErrorType, and Auth.js formats it for server logging.
interview.followUp: What should code inspect to distinguish failures? Use the type property, and inspect cause when structured diagnostic information is needed.

interview.question: How can an application recognize an AuthError?
interview.answer: Use instanceof AuthError in a catch block to identify an Auth.js authentication failure. After identifying it, the application can use error.type to choose an appropriate handling path.
interview.followUp: Why should unrelated errors be rethrown? They do not belong to Auth.js’s documented error hierarchy and may indicate programming or infrastructure defects.

interview.question: What diagnostic information can AuthError carry?
interview.answer: AuthError can have an optional cause property. That cause is a record of unknown values and includes an optional err field containing an Error.
interview.followUp: How does AuthError relate to specialized failures? Auth.js defines more specific error classes that extend AuthError, so an AuthError check also covers those subclasses.

interview.question: When does the `authorized` callback run, and what can it return?
interview.answer: The `authorized` callback is invoked when Middleware must authorize a request. It receives `auth` and `request`; returning a truthy authorization result permits the request, while a custom `NextResponse` can implement explicit handling.
interview.followUp: How would you return an API error instead of redirecting? Return `NextResponse.json(...)` with an appropriate HTTP status from the callback.

interview.question: How do you protect a route for signed-in users?
interview.answer: Use the `auth` parameter to inspect the authenticated user or token. For a simple protected route, return whether `auth` exists; for more specific rules, inspect its properties before deciding.
interview.followUp: How can the request affect authorization? Read method, URL, or other request data from `request`, then return a boolean or custom response based on those values.

interview.question: What parameters are available to `authorized`?
interview.answer: The callback receives a parameter object containing `auth` and `request`. `auth` represents the current authenticated user or token, while `request` is the Next.js request being authorized.
interview.followUp: What is a useful method-specific policy? Permit a valid token for a POST request and return a 401 JSON response when validation fails.

Awaitable.summary: Awaitable<T> is Auth.js's public type for a result that can be supplied immediately as T or asynchronously through PromiseLike<T>. It lets callbacks and provider hooks support either synchronous or asynchronous implementations.
Awaitable.explanation: Awaitable<T> is a union that permits either a value of type T or a PromiseLike<T>. Auth.js uses it for extension points such as callbacks, allowing implementations to complete immediately or return a thenable that resolves to the declared result.

interview.question: What does Awaitable<T> represent?
interview.answer: Awaitable<T> means T or PromiseLike<T>. It lets an Auth.js callback return its result directly or asynchronously while preserving the result type.
interview.followUp: How would a consumer handle both forms? Use await: JavaScript assimilates thenables, so awaiting the value produces T.

interview.question: Why would Auth.js use Awaitable for callbacks?
interview.answer: A callback typed as Awaitable<string> may return a string immediately or a promise-like object resolving to a string. This supports both synchronous and asynchronous implementations without separate callback types.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful in library APIs? Callers can provide lightweight synchronous handlers while still supporting I/O-bound handlers.

interview.question: What is the exact declaration of Awaitable?
interview.answer: The declaration is `type Awaitable<T> = T | PromiseLike<T>`. The generic parameter T is the eventual logical result, while the union permits either immediate or deferred delivery.
interview.followUp: How does it differ from `Promise<T>`? `Promise<T>` requires a promise object; Awaitable<T> also accepts T directly and any compatible thenable.

keyPoints: Awaitable is documented as a public type in the core package's types module.
Its generic T describes the result type shared by both allowed branches.
Auth.js applies Awaitable to callback return types such as redirect, whose result is a string.
JWT callbacks can return either immediately or asynchronously, with null or JWT as the result.
gotchas: Awaitable is broader than Promise<T>: synchronous values are valid, and the asynchronous branch is PromiseLike<T>, not only native Promise<T>.

interview.question: How do you configure a custom Auth.js base path?

interview.question: What are Auth.js callbacks?
interview.answer: Callbacks are asynchronous functions configured in Auth.js to control what happens during authentication actions. They can implement access controls and integrate with databases or APIs.
interview.followUp: Which callback controls client-visible session data? The session callback does, and its return value is exposed to the client.

interview.question: When does the jwt callback run, and what is its role?
interview.answer: The jwt callback runs when a JWT is created at sign-in or updated when the client accesses a session. Values returned by it are saved in the JWT and can then be forwarded by the session callback.
interview.followUp: How would you expose a token property? Return that property from the session callback as part of the session object.

interview.question: How does signIn control authentication?
interview.answer: The signIn callback determines whether sign-in continues. Returning true continues, returning false or throwing stops the flow and redirects to the error page, while returning a string redirects to that URL.
interview.followUp: How can access be restricted by email domain? Inspect the profile in signIn and return whether its email ends with the permitted domain.

keyPoints: Configure callbacks as asynchronous functions that customize Auth.js behavior during authentication actions.
Callbacks can enforce access rules even when the application does not use a database.
The jwt callback stores its returned token data and makes it available to the session callback.
The redirect callback runs when Auth.js redirects a user to a callback URL, including sign-in and sign-out.
A true result from signIn permits the sign-in process to continue.
A false result or thrown error rejects the sign-in flow and sends the user to the error page.

interview.question: What does the credentials property control?

interview.followUp: Why does the input definition affect authorize? The same keys determine the Partial<Record<keyof CredentialsInputs, unknown>> shape passed to the callback.

interview.question: How does authorize determine whether sign-in succeeds?

interview.question: What is the expected function shape?
interview.answer: The function accepts the same input and optional initialization arguments as fetch and returns Promise<Response>. This lets the implementation add transport behavior while preserving the expected Web Fetch contract.

interview.question: When is overriding fetch useful?

interview.question: How do you enable Auth.js debugging?

interview.question: How can debugging output be customized?
interview.answer: Provide a `logger` object with `error`, `warn`, and `debug` methods in the Auth.js configuration. Those methods receive a code and additional message values, allowing output to be sent to another service or reformatted.
interview.followUp: What happens if both options are configured? The custom logger wins and the `debug` option is ignored.

interview.question: Why should debug logging be restricted in production?
interview.answer: Debug output can include authentication and database requests and responses, as well as errors. Because those details may expose sensitive information, production logs must be handled carefully.
interview.followUp: What is a safer default? Enable debugging only outside production and sanitize any diagnostic data that is retained.

interview.question: How do you configure Descope in Auth.js?

interview.followUp: What callback route must Descope allow? The authorized callback is https://example.com/api/auth/callback/descope, adapted to the application's origin.

interview.question: Which Descope values are required?
interview.answer: The client ID comes from the final segment of the Descope issuer or the project ID, the client secret is the Descope access key, and the issuer is the OIDC issuer URL. These values can be supplied through AUTH_DESCOPE_ID, AUTH_DESCOPE_SECRET, and AUTH_DESCOPE_ISSUER.
interview.followUp: Why use an issuer? It lets the OIDC provider configuration identify the Descope authorization server and its endpoints.

interview.question: What does the Descope provider return?
interview.answer: The provider is exposed as Descope from @auth/core/providers/descope and is called with an OIDCUserConfig containing the provider settings. Its return type is OIDCConfig<DescopeProfile>.
interview.followUp: How can defaults be changed? Pass provider configuration overrides to the factory; Auth.js documents customizing built-in OAuth providers for that purpose.

interview.question: What is the purpose of Auth.js events?

interview.followUp: What should an event handler do with its message? Inspect it according to the specific event and flow, because the message shape is not uniform.

interview.question: What can an event message contain?

interview.question: What does getCsrfToken return?
interview.answer: It is an asynchronous zero-argument function whose result is a Promise<string>. The string is the current CSRF token used for state-changing requests.
interview.followUp: Why is the token needed? Auth.js uses the double-submit-cookie technique, comparing the submitted token with the value associated with the cookie.

interview.question: When should an application call getCsrfToken?
interview.answer: Use it when a request changes state, including authentication actions or session updates. Retrieve the token with await and submit it as part of the request or form data.
interview.followUp: What should happen if Auth.js CSRF protection is disabled? A CSRF response may be unavailable and the corresponding endpoint can return 404.

interview.question: What is the function signature and how is it used?
interview.answer: The function takes no parameters, so its signature is getCsrfToken(): Promise<string>. The caller must await the promise before using the token value.
interview.followUp: What broader security mechanism does this support? It supports CSRF prevention through a double-submit cookie rather than accepting an unverified state-changing request.

keyPoints: The function resolves to the currently available CSRF token.

interview.followUp: How would you protect a route? Check the session or its user, redirect when it is absent, and call next only for an authenticated request.

interview.question: What are getSession's parameters and return type?
interview.answer: The request is the required input, while the Auth.js Express configuration supplies the authentication settings. The function returns GetSessionResult, which represents the resolved session result.
interview.followUp: Why pass configuration explicitly? The Express API needs the application’s Auth.js configuration to evaluate the request against the configured authentication setup.

interview.question: How is getSession commonly used in Express?
interview.answer: A common pattern is middleware that assigns await getSession(req) to res.locals.session, followed by route handlers that read that value. This makes session data available across routes and to template rendering.
interview.followUp: How should a route handle a missing session? Test for session?.user and redirect to login instead of rendering protected content.

interview.followUp: Why is the route path catch-all? It lets the handler receive the multiple authentication paths used by provider callbacks and Auth.js endpoints.

interview.question: How do you connect `handlers` to the application route?
interview.answer: The configuration belongs in an `auth.ts` file, where `NextAuth` is initialized and `handlers` is exported. The route module then imports that export and maps its methods to `GET` and `POST`.
interview.followUp: What other values can the same initialization export? Auth.js also exposes methods such as `auth`, `signIn`, and `signOut`, depending on the application’s needs.

interview.question: What kinds of requests do the handler methods serve?
interview.answer: The exported methods expose endpoints for OAuth and email providers as well as Auth.js REST endpoints such as the session endpoint. They are intended to be re-exported after Auth.js has been initialized.
interview.followUp: How would you add custom application behavior? Keep the Auth.js handler route dedicated to these methods and implement unrelated application routes separately.

interview.question: What do the Auth.js JWT helpers do?
interview.answer: The module exposes `encode` to issue a JWT and `decode` to read an Auth.js-issued JWT. Auth.js encrypts the JWT by default with A256CBC-HS512, deriving the key from the configured secret.
interview.followUp: Why should an Auth.js JWT not normally be sent to an unrelated API? It is designed for use by the application that issued it, so an identity-provider access token is the appropriate credential for a third-party API.

interview.question: How does Auth.js retrieve a JWT from a request?
interview.answer: `getToken` accepts an Auth.js request and returns either the decoded payload or, when requested, the raw JWT string. It searches cookies and the Authorization header for the token.
interview.followUp: What happens when no usable token is found? The function returns `null`, including when a Bearer value has malformed percent-encoding.

interview.question: How is an Auth.js JWT protected?
interview.answer: The secret can come from the `AUTH_SECRET` environment variable or from the `secret` parameter passed to the helper. That secret is used to derive the encryption key for the token.
interview.followUp: What deployment requirement follows from this? The application must provide a cryptographically secure `AUTH_SECRET`; the deployment documentation recommends a random value of at least 32 characters.

keyPoints: The default protection is authenticated encryption with the A256CBC-HS512 JWE algorithm.
The encryption key material comes from the environment secret or an explicitly supplied secret.
`encode` returns a newly issued encrypted token rather than a plaintext payload.
`decode` reads an Auth.js token and resolves its payload when the token and secret are valid.
`getToken` can return structured claims or the original compact token, depending on its options.

Treat the token as an encrypted JWE rather than assuming it is merely a signed, readable JWT.
When retrieving a token from a request, account for both cookie and Authorization-header sources.

interview.question: When does the jwt callback execute, and what happens to its return value?
interview.answer: It runs when Auth.js creates a JWT at sign-in and when the token is updated, including when a client session is accessed. The returned value is stored in the JWT and forwarded to the session callback.
interview.followUp: How would you expose a custom token field to the browser? Return it from jwt, then explicitly assign token.field to a session property in session.

interview.question: How does the token parameter differ on initial and subsequent calls?
interview.answer: The token parameter is a subset of the JWT during sign-in or sign-up, including name, email, and image; on later calls it is the full JWT. The callback may return null or a JWT asynchronously.
interview.followUp: Why should code distinguish initial sign-in from later calls? Initial calls can include user or account data, while later calls generally rely on the persisted token.

interview.question: What security and storage characteristics apply to Auth.js JWT sessions?
interview.answer: JWTs are encrypted by default, and the callback can support access control without a database by persisting claims in the token. Auth.js derives encryption from AUTH_SECRET unless configuration supplies another secret.
interview.followUp: What should be done for a third-party API that needs JWT authentication? Use the identity provider's JWT rather than treating an Auth.js JWT as a general-purpose third-party token.

interview.answer: A custom provider object must identify itself with an `id` and `name`, and specify an OAuth or OIDC `type`. OIDC providers can use an `issuer` so Auth.js can discover the provider's configuration.
interview.followUp: Why is the provider ID significant? It is used by `signIn` and becomes part of the callback URL, so changing it affects integration configuration.

keyPoints: Auth.js includes a large catalog of ready-made integrations, so check built-in providers before implementing one yourself.
A provider does not need to be in the built-in catalog if it follows OAuth or OpenID Connect standards.
Custom integrations are registered by adding a provider object to the `providers` array.
Use `oidc` for OpenID Connect integrations and `oauth` for OAuth 2 providers.
For OIDC, an issuer lets Auth.js locate the provider's well-known discovery document.
Built-in provider settings can be selectively overridden when the provider is called.
gotchas: Built-in providers still require the provider-specific credentials, normally a client ID and client secret.
An OAuth or OIDC provider must be configured with the callback URL generated from its provider ID.

Reddit.summary: Auth.js includes Reddit as a built-in OAuth provider. Configure Reddit credentials in `NextAuth`, and use `duration: "permanent"` when a refresh token is required.
Reddit.explanation: The Reddit provider is a built-in OAuth integration. Add it to Auth.js with Reddit credentials; customize authorization parameters when you need a refresh token rather than the provider's default short-lived access token.

useCases.title: Refresh-token authorization

useCases.title: Built-in OAuth setup
useCases.scenario: A project wants a standard Reddit OAuth integration without implementing provider endpoints itself.

interview.question: How is Reddit added to a Next.js Auth.js configuration?
interview.answer: The provider is imported from `next-auth/providers/reddit` and passed to `NextAuth` through the `providers` array. Credentials can be supplied explicitly with `clientId` and `clientSecret`, or the provider can use the documented environment-variable setup.
interview.followUp: How would you obtain a refresh token? Set `authorization.params.duration` to `"permanent"` in the Reddit provider configuration.

interview.question: What callback URL must be configured for Reddit?
interview.answer: The documented callback URL is `/api/auth/callback/reddit` under the application's origin. That URL must be registered in Reddit's application settings, and Reddit permits only one callback URL per client credential pair.
interview.followUp: What deployment constraint follows from that limitation? A single Reddit credential pair cannot directly serve multiple callback URLs.

interview.question: What are Reddit's default token limitations?
interview.answer: The default template requests only the `identity` scope and provides a one-hour access token. To request a refresh token, configure the authorization parameter `duration` as `permanent`.
interview.followUp: Why is this configuration necessary for durable access? Without the permanent duration parameter, the documented default does not provide the refresh-token behavior needed for renewal.

keyPoints: Auth.js supplies Reddit as a built-in provider rather than requiring a custom OAuth implementation.
The Reddit callback endpoint follows the Auth.js API route pattern and ends with the provider identifier `reddit`.
The getting-started page documents `AUTH_REDDIT_ID` and `AUTH_REDDIT_SECRET` as the provider environment variables.
The provider can be used with its built-in defaults, while explicit options are available for customization.
A refresh token requires changing the authorization settings instead of relying on the default provider configuration.
gotchas: Users must authorize Reddit on every visit through Reddit's authorization page.
A Reddit application can have only one callback URL for each credential pair.
The default access token lasts one hour, so long-lived access requires additional authorization configuration.

redirect callback.summary: The redirect callback controls where Auth.js sends users after callback-URL redirects, such as sign-in or sign-out. Return the requested destination when it meets your policy, or a safe fallback such as `baseUrl`.
redirect callback.explanation: The redirect callback runs when Auth.js sends a user to a callback URL during sign-in or sign-out. It receives the requested URL and the configured base URL, and must return the destination string; the default policy permits only URLs on the origin, while the callback can customize that policy.

parameters.name: baseUrl
parameters.description: Default base URL of the site; can be used as a fallback.

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: Callback URL provided by the client.

example.title: Restrict redirect destinations
example.explanation: Configures Auth.js to accept relative destinations and same-origin absolute URLs while sending other destinations to the site base URL.

useCases.title: Handle relative callback paths
useCases.scenario: Allow a post-authentication path such as `/dashboard` while resolving it against the site's base URL.

useCases.title: Enforce same-origin redirects
useCases.scenario: Permit absolute callback URLs only when their origin matches the configured site.

useCases.title: Provide a safe fallback
useCases.scenario: Send unapproved destinations to the configured site rather than honoring them.

interview.question: What is the redirect callback and when does Auth.js call it?
interview.answer: It is an asynchronous callback with the signature `(params) => Awaitable<string>`. Auth.js invokes it whenever a user is redirected to a callback URL, including sign-in and sign-out, and the returned string is the destination.
interview.followUp: What inputs does it receive? It receives `url`, supplied by the client as the callback URL, and `baseUrl`, the site's default base URL.

interview.question: What parameters are available to the redirect callback?
interview.answer: The callback receives `url` and `baseUrl`. `url` is the client-provided callback URL, while `baseUrl` is the site's default base URL and can serve as a fallback.
interview.followUp: How can a callback safely handle relative URLs? Prefix a leading-slash path with `baseUrl` before returning it.

interview.question: How would you implement an origin-restricted redirect policy?
interview.answer: A common policy accepts paths beginning with `/`, accepts absolute URLs whose origin equals `baseUrl`, and returns `baseUrl` for everything else. This preserves relative and same-origin navigation while rejecting other destinations.
interview.followUp: Why reject other origins? Falling back to `baseUrl` prevents the callback from authorizing destinations outside the configured site origin.

keyPoints: The redirect callback is an asynchronous customization point for Auth.js actions.
It participates in both sign-in and sign-out redirection flows.
Auth.js applies a same-host restriction by default.
Override the callback when the application's redirect policy needs to differ from the default.
Use `baseUrl` as the canonical site destination or as the fallback for rejected URLs.
Inspect `url` to evaluate the destination requested by the client.
The callback's return value directly specifies the redirect destination.
gotchas: Do not assume arbitrary external callback URLs are accepted; the documented default restricts redirects to the origin's host.
Always return a valid destination string, because the returned value determines where the browser is redirected.

Resend.summary: Resend is an Auth.js passwordless email provider that sends magic links with verification tokens. It requires a database adapter, a verified sending domain, and a Resend API key.
Resend.explanation: Resend is Auth.js’s passwordless email provider. It sends a verification link containing a token; the token is stored through a database adapter and, when followed before expiry, signs the user in or creates the account.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional provider settings, including the sending address and API key; the documented example configures `from`.

useCases.scenario: Use Resend’s email delivery service for Auth.js verification messages.

interview.question: How does Resend authenticate a user?
interview.answer: Resend implements passwordless authentication by emailing a verification token inside a sign-in URL. A valid link signs in an existing account or creates a new account for the email address.
interview.followUp: Why is a database required? The verification token must be stored, so email authentication cannot be enabled without a database adapter.

interview.question: How long is the verification token valid by default?
interview.answer: The default token lifetime is 24 hours. The user must follow the emailed link during that period for the token to be accepted.
interview.followUp: How would you change the lifetime? Configure the email provider’s maxAge according to the broader Auth.js email-provider configuration.

interview.question: What setup is required before enabling Resend?
interview.answer: Configure a database adapter, add a verified Resend domain, generate an API key, and expose it as AUTH_RESEND_KEY. Then register Resend in the providers array and configure a suitable from address.
interview.followUp: What happens if the environment variable is renamed? Pass the renamed value explicitly in the Resend provider configuration.

keyPoints: Resend provides passwordless sign-in by sending users magic links containing verification tokens.
A verification token normally expires after 24 hours.
Following a valid link can create the user account and immediately establish the sign-in.
Resend can be offered alongside OAuth providers or used as the sole authentication option.
The Resend API key is conventionally supplied through AUTH_RESEND_KEY.
Using the conventional variable name lets the provider discover the API key without extra configuration.
gotchas: A database adapter is still mandatory even when sessions use JSON Web Tokens, because email verification tokens need persistence.
Verify the sending domain in Resend and use an address from that domain in `from`.
Renaming AUTH_RESEND_KEY requires explicitly supplying the alternative environment variable value to the provider.

Salesforce.summary: Auth.js includes Salesforce as a built-in OAuth/OIDC provider. Add it to the provider list, set the Salesforce client credentials, and register the documented callback URL in Salesforce.
Salesforce.explanation: Salesforce is a built-in OAuth/OIDC provider. Add the provider to Auth.js, configure the Salesforce client credentials through the documented environment variables, and register Auth.js’s callback URL in Salesforce.

example.title: Configure Salesforce with NextAuth
example.explanation: Registers Salesforce as a built-in Auth.js provider; credentials are read from the documented environment variables.

useCases.title: Connect an Auth.js application to Salesforce user accounts
useCases.scenario: Enterprise identity

useCases.scenario: Multi-provider authentication

interview.question: How do you add Salesforce authentication to a Next.js Auth.js application?
interview.answer: Use the built-in Salesforce provider in the Auth.js providers list. In a Next.js setup, import it from `next-auth/providers/salesforce` and pass `Salesforce` to `NextAuth({ providers: [...] })`.
interview.followUp: What configuration is needed beyond the provider declaration? Define `AUTH_SALESFORCE_ID` and `AUTH_SALESFORCE_SECRET`, then register the correct callback URL with Salesforce.

interview.question: Which environment variables does the Salesforce provider use?
interview.answer: The documented environment variables are `AUTH_SALESFORCE_ID` and `AUTH_SALESFORCE_SECRET`. Auth.js uses these values for the Salesforce client configuration.
interview.followUp: How would you customize provider behavior? Call the provider function with options and override the defaults, which Auth.js deeply merges with the built-in configuration.

interview.question: What callback URL must be configured for Salesforce?
interview.answer: For Next.js, the callback URL is `https://example.com/api/auth/callback/salesforce`. This URL must also be entered as the redirect URI in the Salesforce application settings.
interview.followUp: What changes for other integrations? The provider page documents `/auth/callback/salesforce` for Qwik and SvelteKit, while the Next.js path includes `/api`.

keyPoints: Auth.js supplies Salesforce as a built-in provider rather than requiring a custom OAuth implementation.
Set the Salesforce client ID and secret using the provider-specific environment variable names.
The Next.js callback endpoint follows Auth.js’s API callback route and includes the Salesforce provider ID.
The built-in defaults handle the standard provider configuration for the normal integration path.

secret.summary: `secret` is the Auth.js configuration value used to hash tokens, sign cookies, and generate cryptographic keys. Provide a random string or an ordered array to support secret rotation.
secret.explanation: Auth.js uses the secret to hash tokens, sign cookies, and derive cryptographic keys. You can supply one secret or an ordered array: the first secret able to decrypt an existing JWT is selected, while the first array entry protects newly created sessions.

parameters.name: secret
parameters.description: A random string, or an array of secrets used for token hashing, cookie signing, cryptographic keys, and JWT decryption.

example.title: Configure an Auth.js secret
example.explanation: Set AUTH_SECRET in the environment, then pass it explicitly to the Auth.js configuration.

useCases.title: Single-secret authentication configuration
useCases.scenario: A standard deployment needs one stable value for protecting authentication state.

useCases.title: Secret rotation
useCases.scenario: A team must replace a compromised or aging secret without invalidating every existing session at once.

useCases.title: Environment-based JWT protection
useCases.scenario: A deployment wants JWT encryption enabled through conventional environment configuration.

interview.question: What does the Auth.js secret protect?
interview.answer: The secret is used to hash tokens, sign cookies, and generate cryptographic keys. Auth.js also uses it for JWT encryption by default.
interview.followUp: How can secrets be rotated without immediately invalidating sessions? Supply an array with the newest secret first; Auth.js tries the entries for decryption and uses the first entry for new sessions.

interview.question: What values can the `secret` option accept?
interview.answer: The configuration type is `string | string[]`. A single string is sufficient for normal operation, while an array supports key rotation.
interview.followUp: What ordering is required during rotation? Put the newer secret at index zero so newly issued sessions use it.

interview.question: How should a production secret be generated and supplied?
interview.answer: The `AUTH_SECRET` environment variable is the conventional deployment setting, and the CLI can generate a random value with `npx auth secret`. The deployment documentation recommends a cryptographically secure random string of at least 32 characters.
interview.followUp: Why prefer environment configuration? It keeps the secret outside source code and allows deployment-specific values.

keyPoints: The `secret` configuration accepts either one string or an array of strings.
Auth.js uses the value for token hashing, cookie signing, and cryptographic-key generation.
JWT encryption is enabled by default when Auth.js obtains the secret from `AUTH_SECRET`.
The deployment-level secret protects cookies and tokens during authentication.
Generate a suitable secret with the Auth.js CLI rather than inventing a predictable value.
Among Auth.js environment variables, `AUTH_SECRET` is the only one documented as strictly required.
gotchas: When rotating secrets, place the newest value first so new sessions use it; older values can remain available for decrypting existing JWTs.

interview.question: How does the Sendgrid provider authenticate a user?
interview.answer: Sendgrid implements passwordless email authentication by sending a link containing a verification token. The token is stored through the configured database adapter and, when used, Auth.js creates or signs in the account.
interview.followUp: Why is the adapter mandatory? The verification token must be persisted so Auth.js can validate the link during the later request.

interview.question: What storage configuration is required?
interview.answer: The provider can use JWT-managed or database-managed sessions, but email sign-in still needs a database adapter. The adapter stores the email verification token used during the sign-in flow.
interview.followUp: Can a JWT session replace the adapter? No; the session strategy and token persistence solve different parts of the flow.

interview.question: How is the Sendgrid API key configured?
interview.answer: Auth.js automatically reads the API key from AUTH_SENDGRID_KEY. If the key uses another environment-variable name, pass that value as the provider's apiKey option.
interview.followUp: What other provider setting must be configured for delivery? Set from to an address whose domain has been added to the Sendgrid account.

keyPoints: Sendgrid provides passwordless sign-in by emailing a magic link containing a verification token.
Unless configured otherwise, the emailed verification token expires after 24 hours.
Redeeming the link within its validity period creates the account when needed and signs the user in.
Sendgrid supports both JWT-based and database-based session management.
After setup, the built-in sign-in endpoint starts the email flow when given an email address.
Store the Sendgrid API key in AUTH_SENDGRID_KEY for the provider's automatic environment-variable discovery.

The sender domain must first be added to Sendgrid, and the `from` address must use that domain.

SequelizeAdapter.explanation: SequelizeAdapter connects Auth.js to a Sequelize database client. Calling it returns an Auth.js Adapter that supplies persistence for users, accounts, sessions, and related authentication data through Sequelize models.

parameters.name: client
parameters.description: Configured Sequelize database client used by the adapter.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional Sequelize adapter configuration.

example.explanation: Creates a Sequelize client from the database URL and supplies the resulting adapter to Auth.js.

useCases.title: Integrate with an existing Sequelize setup

useCases.title: Use migrations for the authentication schema
useCases.scenario: A team needs Auth.js tables managed predictably across deployment environments.

interview.question: What does SequelizeAdapter do?
interview.answer: SequelizeAdapter is a factory that accepts a Sequelize client and returns an Auth.js Adapter. Auth.js then uses that adapter to persist authentication data through Sequelize.
interview.followUp: What must be supplied to the factory? A configured Sequelize instance, typically initialized with the application database connection string.

interview.question: What parameters does SequelizeAdapter accept?
interview.answer: Its required parameter is `client`, whose type is `Sequelize`. An optional `options` parameter can customize adapter behavior.
interview.followUp: Why pass a client instead of a connection string? The adapter relies on the already configured Sequelize instance and its database dialect, connection, and models.

interview.question: How should the database schema be provisioned?
interview.answer: The adapter package does not create database tables by default. Production deployments should create the required schema with migrations; development can use `sequelize.sync()`.
interview.followUp: What is the tradeoff of `sequelize.sync()`? It is convenient for development, but migrations provide controlled and repeatable schema changes for production.

keyPoints: The package is Auth.js's official Sequelize integration.
The API exposes a Sequelize adapter options interface for optional configuration.
The adapter defines Sequelize models for Auth.js data that is stored in the database.
gotchas: The adapter does not automatically create the required database tables.
Use database migrations to provision tables in production rather than relying on runtime synchronization.
Installing Sequelize and the adapter is not sufficient; the selected database driver is a separate dependency.

const { data: session } = useSession()
session.returns: The current session object when an authenticated session exists; otherwise null or another falsy result, depending on the integration.

example.explanation: Call the exported auth function on the server and use the returned session when it exists.

useCases.title: Gate protected resources

interview.question: How do you read the current session on the server?
interview.answer: On the server, use the auth function returned from NextAuth and exported from the Auth.js configuration. It provides the current session, which can then be checked before rendering protected content.
interview.followUp: How would you read it in a client component? Use useSession(), but ensure SessionProvider wraps the component tree.

interview.question: What is required to use useSession() in a client component?
interview.answer: useSession() is the client-side session hook. It should be used beneath SessionProvider, which supplies session state to descendant components.
interview.followUp: What should a protected client view do while the session is unresolved? Handle the loading state before deciding whether to render authenticated or unauthenticated content.

interview.question: What does a session lookup return when no user is signed in?
interview.answer: The session endpoint returns the user's session when one exists and null otherwise. Session checks can therefore distinguish an authenticated request from one without an active session.
interview.followUp: How can the result be used for route protection? Redirect or return an unauthenticated response when no valid session is present.

Client components can retrieve session data with useSession together with SessionProvider.
Pages Router components can receive a session obtained by the page and passed through component props.
In SvelteKit-style routes, the session is available from event.sharedMap, while clients use useSession().

Do not assume custom session fields are stored in the database; database sessions persist the session record, not the complete session object.

Session.explanation: Session describes the currently authenticated user and is returned by Auth.js session-reading APIs such as `auth`, `useSession`, and `getSession`. Its default user data is intentionally limited; additional fields must be explicitly transferred through the appropriate callbacks.

interview.question: What is the Auth.js Session interface used for?
interview.answer: The Session interface represents the active session of the logged-in user. It is returned by `auth`, `useSession`, and `getSession`, and can also be received through the `SessionProvider` context.
interview.followUp: How would you add a user ID? Add it to the JWT in the `jwt` callback, then copy it to `session.user.id` in the `session` callback so client-facing session reads include it.

interview.question: Which user fields are included by default?
interview.answer: By default, Auth.js exposes only a limited subset of user information in the session: `name`, `email`, and `image`. This minimizes the risk of accidentally exposing sensitive user data.
interview.followUp: Why is an explicit callback needed for extra fields? Data placed in the token is not automatically exposed to the client; the session callback must return the desired field.

interview.question: How do the session strategies differ?
interview.answer: Auth.js supports JWT and database session strategies. JWT is the default unless a database provider is configured; with JWT, the session is represented by an encrypted token in an HttpOnly cookie, while database sessions store a session record and put its identifier in the cookie.
interview.followUp: How can the default be overridden? Configure `session.strategy` explicitly as either `"jwt"` or `"database"`.

keyPoints: The interface is available through server and client session access APIs, including `auth`, `useSession`, and `getSession`.
The default session intentionally exposes only selected user information rather than the complete user record.
The default user fields are name, email, and image.
TypeScript module augmentation lets an application add custom properties to the shared Session type.
After callback configuration, both server-side `auth()` and client-side `useSession()` can expose a user ID.

interview.question: When does the session callback run, and what does it control?
interview.answer: It runs whenever Auth.js checks a session, such as through the session endpoint, `useSession`, or `getSession`. Its returned value is the session data exposed to the client.
interview.followUp: How would you expose a value stored by the JWT callback? Return the session after copying the value from `token` onto the appropriate session property.

interview.question: Which callback parameters depend on the session strategy?
interview.answer: With JWT sessions, the callback can receive `token`; with database sessions, it can receive `user`. The callback should return the session object, optionally enriched with approved data.
interview.followUp: What changes when switching from JWT to database sessions? Replace token-based enrichment with data obtained from the `user` argument or a database lookup.

interview.question: Why must the session callback explicitly return custom JWT fields?
interview.answer: The callback determines which session fields are sent to the client. Fields added to the JWT must be explicitly copied into the returned session, and only a subset is returned by default for security.
interview.followUp: How should sensitive provider tokens be handled? Expose them only when required and validate the client-facing design because the returned session is public to the client.

keyPoints: Auth.js invokes it during session checks, including common client and server session access paths.
The object returned from the callback defines the client-visible session shape.
Auth.js intentionally limits the default token-to-session exposure.
The callback can perform database access when session enrichment requires additional data.
A common use is copying a database user ID into `session.user.id`.
gotchas: Anything returned by the callback can reach the client, so do not include secrets or other sensitive data.
Adding a property in `jwt` alone does not expose it; copy it onto the returned session.
Do not assume both `token` and `user` are available: their presence depends on the configured session strategy.

session event.explanation: The session event is an asynchronous handler invoked when Auth.js processes a session event. It receives a message whose contents depend on the authentication flow and session strategy, so it is suitable for audit logging rather than changing the response.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the Auth.js session event?
interview.answer: The session event is configured under the Auth.js events option as an asynchronous function receiving a message. It runs when a session event occurs and is intended for side effects such as audit logging, not for returning a response.
interview.followUp: How should the handler be designed for different session strategies? Inspect the message according to the configured flow because it may contain a JWT token or an adapter-backed session object.

interview.question: What does the session event handler return?
interview.answer: Its signature is `(message) => Awaitable<void>`. The callback does not produce a response; it receives event information and completes asynchronously.
interview.followUp: What if application code needs to alter data exposed in the session? That is a different concern from this event handler and should use the appropriate session configuration callback.

interview.question: What can the session event message contain?
interview.answer: The message depends on the authentication flow, including whether the application uses OAuth or email authentication and JWT or database sessions. It typically contains a user and/or token-related information.
interview.followUp: Which session-specific values can appear? With JWT sessions the message can contain `token`; with database-persisted sessions it can contain `session` from the adapter.

interview.followUp: Which environment variable has the same purpose? `AUTH_TRUST_HOST=true` is the environment-variable equivalent of `trustHost: true`.

interview.answer: Wikimedia supports multiple projects, including Wikipedia, Wikidata, Wikibooks, and Wiktionary. The provider therefore represents Wikimedia OAuth access across those projects rather than only one site.
interview.followUp: What permission choice is appropriate for sign-in only? Select the identity-verification-only scope unless page reading or user actions are required.

interview.question: How do you configure WordPress authentication in Auth.js?
interview.answer: The provider can be added directly as WordPress in a framework configuration, or called as WordPress({ clientId, clientSecret }) in the core API. Auth.js uses the provider's built-in defaults unless you override them.
interview.followUp: How would you customize it? Pass provider options to the function and merge them with the built-in defaults, changing only the settings required by the WordPress installation.

interview.question: Which package import and environment variables are used?
interview.answer: For a Next.js setup, import WordPress from next-auth/providers/wordpress and include it in the providers array passed to NextAuth. The documented environment variables are AUTH_WORDPRESS_ID and AUTH_WORDPRESS_SECRET.
interview.followUp: What must be configured outside the application? The WordPress client must be registered with the callback URL https://example.com/api/auth/callback/wordpress.

interview.question: What are the WordPress provider factory's parameter and return types?
interview.answer: The core provider factory accepts an OAuthUserConfig<Record<string, any>> configuration object and returns an OAuthConfig<Record<string, any>>. The configuration can provide client credentials and overrides for the default OAuth setup.
interview.followUp: Why is the return type useful? It supplies the normalized provider definition that Auth.js consumes in its providers configuration.

keyPoints: Auth.js includes WordPress as a built-in provider rather than requiring a custom OAuth provider definition.
For Next.js, register the provider callback at /api/auth/callback/wordpress on the application's origin.

gotchas: The integration assumes WordPress uses OAuth 2 by default; override the built-in configuration if your deployment requires different OAuth settings.

interview.question: What is XataAdapter used for?

interview.followUp: What must be supplied to the adapter? A generated XataClient instance, passed as the adapter's argument.

interview.question: How do you configure XataAdapter in Auth.js?
interview.answer: Install the @auth/xata-adapter package, create a XataClient, and configure adapter: XataAdapter(client) in the Auth.js options.
interview.followUp: How would you initialize the Xata project? Use the Xata CLI with a schema file via xata init --schema=./path/to/your/schema.json.

interview.question: How is the Xata database prepared?
interview.answer: The documented setup uses an Auth.js schema and initializes a Xata project with the Xata CLI. The CLI command accepts the path to that schema file.
interview.followUp: Why is the schema needed? It provides the database structure that the Xata adapter expects for Auth.js data.
